day.title: The morning after the release
day.story: Last night the new price list went live. At 7:40, Mr. Tanyi Godlove at Mile 4 sends a voice note: the website says Palm Oil 5L costs 6 FCFA! You put the old price list back first, so customers see the right prices. Then you reproduce the bug on your laptop. The new file writes prices as text, like "6,600", and the code stopped reading at the comma.
day.lesson: Stay calm. Protect customers first, then reproduce the bug, then fix it, and add a test so it can never come back quietly.

day.title: Review a teammate's pull request
day.story: A teammate adds an "Out of stock" badge to the catalogue and asks for your review. You read every line and run it. It only checks stock at the Nkwen branch, so Bafoussam customers would see the wrong badge. You leave a kind comment: what you saw, why it matters, and a suggested test. She fixes it in ten minutes.
day.lesson: Review the code, not the person. Google's public review guide says to approve a change once it clearly makes the code better, because "there is no such thing as 'perfect' code".

day.title: A call from Bafoussam
day.story: Mr. Kenfack Roland, manager of Bafoussam Centre, calls: "Customers travel far. They want to know if rice is in stock before they come." Before you write any code, you ask questions. Which products? One branch or all four? Must it be an exact number, or is "in stock / low / out" enough? You write his request back in three sentences. He replies: "Yes, exactly that."
day.lesson: A lot of wasted code comes from a request nobody understood. Ask first, write it down, then build.

day.title: "I paid, but my order says pending"
day.story: A wholesale customer paid 72,010 FCFA with MTN Mobile Money for two bags of Rice 50kg. His phone says the payment worked, but the order still says "pending". You read the payment provider's API docs. Your server never received the provider's confirmation message. So you ask the provider for the payment status: successful. Only then do you mark the order as paid.
day.lesson: Code that handles money checks with the payment provider. It never trusts a screenshot or a customer's screen.

day.title: AI as a helper, not the boss
day.story: You are stuck on an error, so you open an AI assistant. Before pasting your code, you remove the secret API key and a customer's phone number. The answer looks confident. You test it on a basket you added up by hand, and it is wrong when a quantity is more than one. You keep the idea, fix that line, and say in your pull request how AI helped.
day.lesson: AI is a fast helper, but you are the engineer. Keep secrets out of it, test what it gives you, and explain every line you keep.

day.title: "The website is too slow on my phone"
day.story: Mrs. Fon Lydia at Commercial Avenue says the website takes forever to open on her phone. In the browser's DevTools you slow the network down to 3G and watch. One huge product photo blocks everything. You resize the images and let them load only when they are needed. On 3G, the page now appears quickly.
day.lesson: Build for the phone your customers really have and the data they can really afford. Jumia and Konga built lighter web apps for users on 2G for exactly this reason.

day.title: No network on the road
day.story: A sales rep calls from a shop on the road to Bafoussam. There is no network, and she took three orders this morning. Are they lost? You check the rep app. It saved each order on the phone, with its own ID, and will send them when the signal comes back. The server ignores any copy it has already received, so nothing is ordered twice.
day.lesson: On the road, a lost signal is normal, not rare. Good apps save first, sync later, and never create double orders.

day.title: Head office asks a stock question
day.story: Head office asks: "Which products are running low at Bafoussam Centre?" Stock is in one table and product names are in another. You write a SQL query that joins them and sorts by quantity. Then you check one product by hand against the branch's own count. You save the query, so next week the answer is one click away.
day.lesson: Answer from the data, not from memory. Check one row by hand before you trust the rest.

day.title: Deploy the fix
day.story: This morning's price fix has been reviewed and approved. You merge it. The pipeline runs every test again; all green, so it puts the new version live. You open the real website on your own phone and check that Palm Oil 5L shows 6,600 FCFA. Then you message Mr. Tanyi: "Fixed, and a test now guards it."
day.lesson: Good deploys are boring, because tests and small changes make them safe. When GOV.UK made tested changes go live automatically, the time from test to live fell from 3 days to half a day.

myths.claim: You need a computer science degree to get a software job.
myths.explain: We read 64 real entry-level adverts. Only 25 of them (39%) strictly required a technical degree. Many said "or equivalent experience", and littlefish in South Africa welcomed bootcamp and self-taught people with a portfolio. A degree can help, but proof matters most: projects you built and can explain.

myths.claim: Testing is one of the skills employers ask juniors for most often.
myths.explain: Testing appeared in 41 of the 64 adverts we read (64%), more than any other skill. That is why you write your first automated test in Chapter 2, not at the end of the track.

myths.claim: AI will soon write all the code, so engineers who understand code won't be needed.
myths.explain: 14 of the 64 adverts asked for experience with AI tools, and they still want people who can judge the result. Stripe asks new graduates to "review, refine, and validate all outputs". littlefish wants juniors who can explain AI-written code line by line. Chapter 1 teaches you to use AI openly and check it.

myths.claim: You must learn every programming language before anyone will hire you.
myths.explain: Go deep in one stack first. 30 of the 64 adverts were flexible about the language. Stripe's advert says "new programming languages can be learned if the fundamentals and general knowledge are present". Your second language comes much faster than your first.

myths.claim: In many interviews, how you explain your thinking counts as much as your code.
myths.explain: Thoughtworks says communication is the most important thing it looks at in pair-programming interviews. Shopify advises candidates to think aloud. Monzo's first call with engineers is about a recent project, with no code at all. That is why every project here is explained in writing and on video.

myths.claim: Senior engineers know everything by heart and never search online.
myths.explain: Seniors read docs and search every day. The difference is that they know what to look for and they check what they find. One UK advert wants someone who "reads error messages, checks the docs". Shopify even lets candidates use online documentation in its coding interview.

myths.claim: Frontend is just making things look pretty.
myths.explain: Frontend engineers make pages fast on cheap phones, usable with a screen reader, and safe when the network fails. 9 of the 10 frontend adverts we read asked for performance. In Nigeria, blind users told TechCabal that some bank apps were unusable because buttons had no labels.

myths.claim: Mobile money and bad networks are real engineering problems, not small details.
myths.explain: An internship in Senegal asked for integrating the Wave mobile-money service. Jaza Energy in Lagos asks its mobile intern to build offline storage and data sync. You meet mobile-money docs in Chapter 5, and the Backend and Mobile pathways go deeper.

ladder.title: Software Rookie
ladder.does: Learning the basics: first JavaScript, Git, how the web works, reading error messages. Asking lots of questions.
ladder.trusted: Your own practice and small, guided exercises.
ladder.program: This is where Chapter 1 begins. Every engineer at Nkwen Traders, and every senior you will ever meet, started here.

ladder.title: Junior Software Developer
ladder.does: Builds small features and fixes bugs in one part of the product, writes tests for them, opens pull requests, takes review feedback well and asks for help early.
ladder.trusted: One clear task at a time, with a senior reviewing every pull request before it goes live.
ladder.program: The program's finish line. By the end you'll have reviewed projects with tests and videos, a pathway, a squad project and a portfolio. You'll also have practised every interview stage employers use.

ladder.title: Software Engineer
ladder.does: Owns whole features from the idea to production, chooses the approach without being told, reviews juniors' code and helps fix things when production breaks.
ladder.trusted: A feature or service that customers and money depend on.
ladder.program: Seeds you plant now: code review in Chapter 6, a real deploy in your pathway, and owning one part of the squad project in Chapter 10.

ladder.title: Senior Software Engineer
ladder.does: Turns a vague business problem into a clear technical plan. Designs systems that stay correct under pressure, weighs speed against safety and cost, stays calm during incidents and mentors juniors.
ladder.trusted: Systems that hold the company's money and its customers' trust, and the growth of other engineers.
ladder.program: The habits start now: explaining every project in writing and on video, reviewing others kindly and explaining AI-written code line by line. Chapter 11 adds system design practice.

ladder.title: Staff Engineer / Engineering Lead
ladder.does: Sets the technical direction for several teams, decides what NOT to build, builds and grows the team, and owns reliability and security for the company.
ladder.trusted: The technical direction of a whole organisation.
ladder.program: Far ahead. But every staff engineer once fought their first error message and opened their first pull request, just like you in Chapter 1.

ladder_note: Years are typical, not rules: they vary a lot by company and country. Titles differ too: the junior rung may be called "Graduate Engineer" or "Software Engineer I". What moves people up is proof of skill, the trust they earn and how clearly they explain their work.

senior.javascript: Writes small, readable functions others understand at a glance, and knows the traps (text that looks like a number, rounding money, async timing) before they bite.
senior.html_css: Builds pages that work on a cheap phone on 3G, with only a keyboard and with a screen reader: solid HTML first, then CSS on top.
senior.dom: Keeps the page in step with the data, handles every click, loading and error state, and never lets one broken script freeze the whole page.
senior.http_apis: Reads any API's docs quickly, designs clear endpoints and error messages, and plans for timeouts, retries and the same request arriving twice.
senior.git: Makes small, clear pull requests, reviews other people's code carefully and kindly, and can untangle any messy history without panic.
senior.testing: Writes a failing test before trusting a fix, tests the bad cases (no network, wrong input, empty stock), and keeps the test suite fast and trusted.
senior.sql: Designs tables that keep data correct, writes queries that stay fast as data grows, and checks every change before running it on real data.
senior.backend: Builds services that stay correct under pressure: no double sales, no lost orders, safe deploys and clear logs when something goes wrong.
senior.frontend: Builds components a whole team can reuse, keeps the app fast on cheap phones, and makes every state clear: loading, empty and error.
senior.mobile: Ships apps that survive bad networks, small batteries and old Android phones, and releases updates without breaking users who don't update.
senior.security: Thinks like an attacker: never trusts input, never stores plain passwords, keeps secrets out of code and checks every payment with the provider.
senior.communication: Turns a vague request into a clear plan, explains trade-offs to people who don't code, writes blameless incident notes and mentors juniors.
